title: What is known about 1RB1LA_1LA0RC_1RD1RC_1LE0RC_---0LF_1LE0LA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LA_1LA0RC_1RD1RC_1LE0RC_---0LF_1LE0LA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. Its tape is a few long blocks of 1s separated by single 0s, followed by an alternating tail (10)^k that grows by one copy now and then. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 10,000 steps by the kernel alone and in the first 107 with native_decide; the C simulator finds no halt in the first 109 steps; an exact macro simulator (blocks of 2 cells) finds no halt in the first 1015 steps.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 5,303 cells have been visited and 4,922 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/power
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.286). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.341).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>15</sup> steps
claims.text: An exact macro simulator (blocks of 2 cells) runs 1015 steps without a halt. The macro simulator cuts the tape into blocks of K cells, run-length codes them, and crosses a whole run at once when the head leaves it on the far side in the state it entered with; it agrees with the plain simulator tools/c/tmrun cell for cell.

claims.title: A chain of blocks, the last one halved
claims.text: At the moments the head reaches a new cell on the right in state C, the tape is solid blocks separated by single 0s followed by an alternating tail; successive moments show the last block halved (98, 49, 25, 12, 6, 3 around step 7.58·10<sup>7</sup>) and the block before it growing by the same amount.

claims.title: The halting state, seen from the run
claims.text: In the first 10<sup>8</sup> steps state E was entered 273,805 times, always reading a 1 (E0 halts).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The tape is a chain of long solid blocks separated by single 0s, with an alternating tail; the last block is halved over and over, each half moving into the block before it, and the chain is rebuilt when it runs out.

facts.text: No halt in an exact macro simulator (blocks of 2 cells).
The last solid block is halved again and again, feeding the block before it.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
No halt in the C simulator; 5,303 cells visited.

sections.heading: What the machine does
html: Stop the machine whenever its head first reaches a new cell on the right, in state C. With e for 10, around step 7.6·107:

Between the separating 0s the tape is solid. Each time, the last solid block is halved: 98, 49, 25, 12, 6, 3, and the ones it loses go to the block before it (362, 413, 441, 455). When the last block is used up the alternating tail gains a copy of 10 (170 to 171) and the halving moves one block to the left (then 455 is halved: 230, 116, …). Every so often the whole chain is regrouped into a few blocks of nearly equal length (e 1^849 e 1^844 e 1^165 at step 78,406,810, e 1^317 e 1^316 e 1^633 e 1^590 … at step 88,004,978).

Halving a block means passing over it many times, so the cost of the cycle grows faster than the tape; the width grows like a power of the step count close to 1/3 (fitted exponents 0.29 and 0.34 for the two sides at 109 steps).

sections.heading: Where a halt would have to come from
html: The halting transition is E reading a 0. E is entered from D reading a 0 and from F reading a 0 (both 1LE), so a halt needs one of them to step left from a 0 onto another 0. In the first 108 steps E was entered 273,805 times, every time on a 1, and 270,551 times at least 7 cells from the right end. In the recorded moments above, the 0s between blocks are always single.
A halt would need two adjacent 0s where D or F turns left, for example a block of length 0 between two separators. Whether the halving ever produces one is open.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.286). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.341).
After 109 steps the tape spans 5,303 cells (314 left of the start, 3,953 right), with a density of 1s of 0.928.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: chain of solid blocks, the last one halved again and again
summary: The tape is a chain of long solid blocks separated by single 0s, with an alternating tail; the last block is halved over and over, each half moving into the block before it, and the chain is rebuilt when it runs out.
